title: Concurrency Pitfalls
subtitle: Stale responses, abort, unhandled rejections, forEach

cards.front: Does single-threaded JS still have concurrency?
cards.meaning: Yes — many async operations can be in flight at once. Pitfalls come from completion order, forgotten error handlers, missing cancellation, and APIs that look async-friendly but aren't (.forEach). This unit is about bugs you ship in React/RN/Nest, not inventing threads.

cards.front: Single-threaded — no races?
cards.meaning: Wrong for apps. The danger is usually not multi-threaded memory races. Two async operations were started; the older one finishes after the newer one and still updates UI/state. Completion-order races still happen with many in-flight Promises.

cards.front: Does network latency preserve send order?
cards.meaning: No. Your event loop runs whichever callback becomes ready first. Send order ≠ completion order.

cards.front: Type 'a' then 'ab' — older results win?
cards.meaning: Classic completion-order race: two requests in flight; latency doesn't preserve send order; response for 'a' may arrive after 'ab' and overwrite state with stale data.
cards.example: type a → request A; type ab → request B; B returns setResults(ab); A returns setResults(a) — stale wins

cards.front: Where else does the search-box race show up?
cards.meaning: Tab switching, rapid filter changes, React effect re-runs without cleanup, double-clicked submit, Nest handler using shared mutable cache without versioning.

cards.front: Fix: request id / generation counter?
cards.meaning: Keep a monotonically increasing generation (or latest query). Increment on each new request; after await, only setState if id === latest. Stops applying stale data; doesn't cancel network unless paired with abort. Wasted bandwidth/CPU may continue.
cards.example: let latest = 0; const id = ++latest; const results = await fetchResults(query); if (id !== latest) return;

cards.front: React effect cleanup for fetch race?
cards.meaning: let cancelled = false; in then check !cancelled before setState; cleanup sets cancelled = true on re-run/unmount — ignore stale when query/deps change. Stops applying stale data, not the network work unless paired with abort.

cards.front: AbortController for search?
cards.meaning: Abort previous controller when a new query starts; pass signal to fetch; catch AbortError as expected control flow, not a user-facing failure. Reduces wasted work vs ignore-only.

cards.front: How does AbortController work?
cards.meaning: abort() signals all consumers of that signal. fetch (and many modern APIs) reject with AbortError / DOMException. Treat abort as control flow, not a user-facing failure.

cards.front: Abort vs ignore-stale?
cards.meaning: Abort stops/cancels in-flight I/O where supported; ignore-stale only prevents bad UI updates. Abort reduces waste; a generation check still helps if some APIs can't abort or if multiple code paths can set state. Use both when needed.

cards.front: Why React Query / SWR / RTK Query exist?
cards.meaning: They automate query keys + cancellation / ignore stale. Knowing the manual pattern (request id + AbortController) proves you understand why they exist — don't rely only on library magic without being able to explain query keys / cancel.

cards.front: User types quickly; older shorter-query results flash — what and fix?
cards.meaning: Classic race: multiple requests in flight; completion order ≠ send order; older response overwrites newer state. Fix with a request id/ref that only commits the latest, and/or AbortController to cancel the previous fetch when a new search starts. Libraries like React Query solve this with query keys and cancellation.

cards.front: What is an unhandled Promise rejection?
cards.meaning: A Promise rejects and nothing handles it in time — no .catch, no await inside try/catch on a caller that actually waits. Fire-and-forget async function that throws is a typical leak.
cards.example: async function risky() { throw new Error('boom'); } risky(); // unhandled rejection risk

cards.front: Unhandled rejections in Node vs browsers/RN vs production?
cards.meaning: Node: warnings; can crash the process depending on version / --unhandled-rejections strictness. Browsers/RN: easy to miss; silent failed features; noisy console in dev. Production: works-on-my-machine empty catches elsewhere; ops only see partial symptoms.

cards.front: Every Promise should…?
cards.meaning: Be awaited in try/catch or have an explicit .catch(). Fire-and-forget only when deliberate and visible — still prefer .catch(logError). Example: void saveDraft(data).catch(logError) for an intentional background save.

cards.front: Why is async onclick a common leak?
cards.meaning: button.onclick = async () => { await submit(); } — rejection becomes unhandled unless try/catch inside. Event handlers must catch or route errors to UI.

cards.front: items.forEach(async item => await save(item)); then log done?
cards.meaning: done runs before saves finish — forEach ignores returned Promises, doesn't await. All async visitors are started; their Promises float away (often unhandled if save rejects).
cards.example: items.forEach(async (item) => { await save(item); }); console.log('done'); // done first

cards.front: Why doesn't forEach await?
cards.meaning: forEach expects a sync visitor. It does not inspect or await a returned Promise.

cards.front: Fixes for forEach(async)?
cards.meaning: Sequential: for (const item of items) await save(item). Parallel: await Promise.all(items.map(item => save(item))). Partial OK: await Promise.allSettled(...). Limited concurrency: pool / batch helper.

cards.front: items.map(async ...) without Promise.all?
cards.meaning: You get an array of Promises — must await Promise.all (or allSettled) if you need completion or error handling as one unit. Avoid map(async) without combining if you need completion.

cards.front: What is debounce (concurrency shaping)?
cards.meaning: Run after activity settles — e.g. search: wait until typing pauses. Conceptual: onInput → reset timer → after 300ms quiet → fetch once. Fewer in-flight requests; pairs well with AbortController on the single latest call. Typical UX: search autocomplete. Strongly reduces starts.
cards.notes: Not only a perf micro-optimization — reduces how many async operations you start, which reduces races and server load.

cards.front: What is throttle (concurrency shaping)?
cards.meaning: Run at most once per interval while activity continues — e.g. scroll handlers, resize, some tracking. Conceptual: onScroll → allow one handler per 100ms; drop or coalesce extras. Typical UX: scroll position sync. Caps rate of starts.

cards.front: Debounce vs throttle for concurrency?
cards.meaning: Debounce: fires after a quiet period (typeahead) — fewer starts. Throttle: regularly during continuous events (scroll) — caps rate of starts. Both reduce in-flight async work and race surface. Neither replaces abort/ignore-stale alone if a slow response can still outrun a later one — but fewer flights make races rarer.

cards.front: Debounce setState but fetch every keypress?
cards.meaning: Wrong. Debounce the async start, not only the render. Launching fetch on every keypress still creates races and load.

cards.front: React Strict Mode / effect re-run pitfall?
cards.meaning: Effects may mount→cleanup→mount in dev. Without cleanup (cancelled = true / abort), you double-fetch and risk races.

cards.front: Double-click submit guard?
cards.meaning: Two clicks → two POSTs. Disable the button, use idempotency keys, or an in-flight guard: if (inFlight) return; inFlight = true; try { await submit(); } finally { inFlight = false; }.

cards.front: Shared mutable state in Nest — race?
cards.meaning: Concurrent requests on one Node process share module-level variables. A request-scoped latest flag on a singleton service can cross wires — prefer per-request locals, not globals, for cancellation tokens.

cards.front: This unit vs accidental sequential await?
cards.meaning: Opposite failure mode: the async/await unit is awaiting too serially. Here the failure is too much overlap without coordination.

cards.front: Preferred defense for search / typeahead?
cards.meaning: Debounce + AbortController (+ ignore-stale).

cards.front: Preferred defense for effect load by id?
cards.meaning: Abort or cancelled flag in cleanup.

cards.front: Must apply only latest, can't abort?
cards.meaning: Generation / request id — ignore stale responses even if the network finishes.

cards.front: Must not lose errors — which rule?
cards.meaning: Never bare fire-and-forget. Every Promise has a home: await in try/catch or explicit .catch.

cards.front: Preferred defense for bulk save?
cards.meaning: all / allSettled / pool — not forEach + async.

cards.front: Catching AbortError as a real failure?
cards.meaning: Noisy toasts on every keystroke. Treat abort as expected control flow, not a user-facing failure.

cards.front: Event loop vs this unit?
cards.meaning: Event loop explains when callbacks run; this unit explains which completion is still valid when several are queued. Stale handler closes over / setState wrong generation → race bug.

cards.front: Concurrency-pitfalls interview bar?
cards.meaning: Narrate the search-box race with a timeline; implement ignore-stale and AbortController and contrast them; explain unhandled rejections and every Promise has a home; fix forEach(async) with for...of or Promise.all; position debounce/throttle as concurrency control; name what React Query automates without hand-waving.
